content.comment_body: I'm familiar with managing backlight colors and turning them on. My issue is figuring out how to switch the backlight off when not in use. From various discussions, it seems the backlight lifespan is only around 20,000 hours. Ideally, I'd like the backlight to automatically come back on when a key is pressed; currently, I achieve this by monitoring arrow keys, which must be pressed with the ESC key. To help, I’ve also included an off-delay timer that switches off the backlight. Is there an easier approach? Any advice?

If you set up special flags in the [product_name] program for display illumination, the backlight doesn't switch on automatically when pressing a button. [company_name] has been aware of this issue for years but hasn’t modified this behavior.

While you were typing, I’ve already used a mix of an off-delay timer and monitoring the arrow keys (together with the ESC key) to get the backlight back on. It’s quite a lot of effort just to preserve the backlight, and I was hoping earlier forum posts on the subject might be outdated.

Unfortunately, that's not true. Even with current [product_name] [version_no], the backlight works the same way. The only workaround is to use the cursor keys (ESC + cursor) to turn on a delay, keeping illumination on for a short time.

@ [user_name], The 20,000 hours mentioned by [company_name] refers to the backlight reaching 50% of its original brightness, not total failure. I have several devices with backlights permanently on, and even after more than two years they're still running without overheating or display problems. Recently, I came across a unit installed on a sewage treatment plant over three years ago, where the backlight was set to always on due to poor lighting, and it was still readable. P.S. I replaced the device due to a relay output fault, and the new one had a bright display. If you're worried about display backlight, you can use a [product_name] TDE, where the backlight is easily managed using function keys and a timer.
@ [user_name], If you add a TDE mainly to avoid pressing the ESC key each time, it's quite an expensive solution...

@ [user_name], Yes, using a TDE just to skip pressing ESC is costly. I suggested it because without full details of the project, a TDE could be suitable for users needing both backlight control and protection for the main display. If the project requires menu navigation, TDE simplifies setup. Also, if a failure occurs, replacing the TDE is easier than the main device, and TDE failure doesn’t affect the rest of the system. For reference, I haven’t encountered backlight failures—the installed units have endured tough environments, usually, the main issue is worn relays or voltage surges affecting the power supply.

analysis.insight_summary: Users find it challenging to turn off the display backlight on [product_name] devices when using program-controlled illumination flags. This leads to complex workarounds to prolong backlight life, such as using key combinations and timers, since the backlight doesn't re-activate automatically with any keypress. [company_name] has not resolved this in recent device versions. While some users worry about backlight longevity, others reassure that actual lifespan tends to be adequate, but the solutions remain convoluted.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect a simple, automated method for managing the display backlight—off when not needed, on immediately when any key is pressed—without requiring elaborate programming or workarounds.
